title: Discovering Your Genjokoan Talk 4
speaker: Myoki Raizelah Bayen
summary: The teacher's talk emphasizes the importance of cultivating acceptance and awareness through mindfulness practices, such as working with koans like "Sunface Buddha, Moonface Buddha." By letting go of preconceptions and focusing on the present moment, we can align ourselves with what's truly essential in our lives and tap into a deeper sense of reality. This practice is rooted in the understanding that our conventional views of time and reality are illusions, and that true understanding can only be accessed by embracing the present moment as it is.

*When you ride in a boat and watch the shore, you might assume that the shore is moving.
But when you keep your eyes closely on the boat, you can see the boat moves.

Similarly, if you examine myriad things with a confused mind, and you suppose that your mind and nature are permanent, when you practice intimately and return to where you are, it will be clear that nothing at all is an unchanging self.*
We are the boat.
I am the boat.
We take ourselves to be this solid ground.
I take myself to be solid.
I see the center, or this pivot point around which the world is revolving.
I see the world from this center point, usually through these lenses that I wear.
I believe I'm right and that the world is moving and changing all around me.
It's a very self-centered view.
So Okumura here, in *Realizing Genjokoan*, says it's a mistake to think that the coast is moving rather than the boat.
It is also a mistake to think of the self as a fixed, unchanging subject around which shifting objects revolve.
I don't know about you, but I live much of my life from this fixed view.
I am here.
I have this seemingly solid sense of self, right?
I think that I know who I am.
I believe that what I perceive is correct.
There's a chair here that I'm sitting on.
There's a massage table.
I'm here.
You're there.
And the shore is moving.
I don't know anything outside of what I know, and so I'm left with assuming that what I know is right.
But Okumura explains:
*Because we each have different karma, each of us sees the world differently.
And yet one often thinks my opinion is absolutely right and all other views are wrong.
To open the hand of thought or to stop discriminating is to stop judging things solely on the basis of one's own limited views.
Because any view is the product of a particular set of conditions, circumstances, and experiences, we must give up our own views as absolutely true.*
I love that.
I'm going to say that again.
To open the hand of thought.
He said that a lot in his writing.
To open the mind, to see with new lenses, a fresh perspective, beginner's mind.
To open the hand of thought is to stop discriminating, to stop judging things solely on the basis of one's own limited views.
So for us, we have zazen to support us in what he's suggesting, to give up our views as absolutely true.
When we sit zazen over time, we slowly start to discern our conditioned views.
To me it seems that just seeing them over and over, again and again, my mind repeats itself a lot.
I don't know about you.

Zazen helps me to see and sense that the self changes.

The next section of the Genjokoan reads:
*Firewood becomes ash, and it does not become firewood again.
Yet do not suppose that the ash is the future and the firewood is the past.
You should understand that firewood abides in the phenomenal expression of firewood, which fully includes past and future and is independent of past and future.
Ash abides in the phenomenal expression of ash, which fully includes future and past.
Just as firewood does not become firewood again after it is ash, you do not return to birth after death.*
Dogen is actually one of the few spiritual teachers who writes about time.
He has a whole fascicle in the Shobogenzo devoted to this topic, called "For the Time Being."
And in this particular verse of the Genjokoan, Dogen is offering his teaching on time.
I'm going to quote Okumura again.
He's really been my friend in making the Genjokoan accessible.
I hope he's been as helpful to you.
Okumura says:
*Commonly we think of time as a stream that flows like a river from a beginningless past to an endless future.
We believe we are born and appear in the stream and later die and disappear from the stream.
But in reality, each stage or dharma position can only be experienced in the present moment, and the present moment does not have any length.*
I'm going to say that again.
*In reality, each stage or dharma position can only be experienced in the present moment, and the present moment doesn't have any length.*
So what I hear Okumura saying is that reality can only be experienced right now, in this very moment, in this present moment.
But there isn't actually any present moment, because by the time I say "now," now is gone.
It's already in the past.
So the present moment actually is nothing.
We often believe that the present is the only reality we experience because the past is gone and the future hasn't come.
But what Okumura is saying here is that the present is nothing.
It's nothing.
That's so fascinating to me, because it's almost cliché that Zen is all about being in the moment, right here, right now.
But Okumura goes on to say:
*Still, from this present moment, which is empty and does not exist, the entire past and the entire future are reflected.
This present moment, which has no length, is the only true reality of life as we experience it.
And since everything is always changing at each present moment, everything arises and perishes over and over again.
Each moment, everything is new and fresh.*
So for me, this is an invitation into the present, an invitation to practice presence, to enter this moment.
Essentially, it's an invitation to practice, because the past is our reflections, it's our memories, and the future is our plans, our desires, our projections, our hopes, our dreams.
But actually, those are all just constructs in our mind.
The past and the future only exist as constructs in our mind.
Okumura goes on to say:
*Yet when we open the hand of thought, there it is again.
Yet when we open the hand of thought in zazen, we let go of our story and sit right here, right now, in the present moment.*
Opening the hand of thought, to open our mind, to see things with beginner's mind, to see each moment as fresh and alive.
Isn't this the Genjokoan?

Maybe you're starting to see, as we move through the verses of the Genjokoan, that Dogen basically says the same thing over and over again, each time using different words, different metaphors, different analogies, different stories, but giving us the same message: to show up fully, to actualize the point, to wake up to the present.

I don't have answers, but I know I'll keep practicing with it.
